synopsis: Mine-site light vehicles are pickups, four-wheel-drives and vans used among heavy machines; they share haul roads with trucks weighing roughly a hundred times more, and blind areas plus this size mismatch are central factors in deadly collisions [f11463, f11464, f3588]. The booklet ranks a haul truck crushing a light vehicle in front of it as the highest-harm collision scenario, although berm and dump-edge events rank higher by fatal-event frequency [f3512, f3584]. The detailed US analysis covers 13 haul-truck collisions in January 2005–June 2021, including five light-vehicle cases and one double fatality; other summaries describe five of 13 deaths, leaving an unresolved distinction between incident and death counts [f3073, f3243, f3514, f11467]. All five light-vehicle cases involved forward movement: two trucks started from stationary, two encountered parked light vehicles, and one interaction was head-on; this supports prioritizing detection before moving off, when time-to-collision calculations give no answer [f3516, f3077, f11591, f11473, f11474]. Visibility aids do not eliminate the hazard: two parked pickups had their strobes switched off, one was momentarily hidden by a cab pillar, and another vehicle's flag may have been inadequately illuminated; a reversing dozer also killed a light-vehicle driver at Snapper Mineral Sands Mine on 12 August 2019 [f3080, f3081, f3082, f3116]. Validation therefore calls for sensor-representative light-vehicle surrogates under a haul truck's nose and includes proving-ground controller tests using light vehicles under the MOSH regime dated 11 October 2025; earlier radar work reported 75 m detection in 2005, while the separate on-road FMVSS 127 rule of 9 May 2024 requires AEB on new light vehicles by 1 September 2029 [f13506, f5352, f6368, f1513].
